title: Rites of Passage
objective: After this level you can explain the three stages scholars see in rites of passage, from coming-of-age ceremonies to funerals.
summary: Rites of passage move a person from one status to another. Van Gennep saw three stages: separation, transition and incorporation, visible in a bat mitzvah and a Hindu funeral alike.

cards.headline: Graduations, weddings, funerals: why do big changes come with ceremonies?
cards.body: Every known society marks the big turning points of life. In 1909 a French anthropologist noticed that these ceremonies share a hidden three-part shape.

cards.headline: Ceremonies for crossing over
cards.body: Arnold van Gennep called them rites of passage: ceremonies that move a person from one social or religious status to another. They appear in all known societies, around birth, coming of age, marriage and death. They also do quiet work. They teach people their new roles, reinforce shared values and bring the community together.

cards.headline: Three stages
cards.body: Van Gennep found the same sequence again and again. First, separation: you leave your old status behind. Then transition, the liminal stage, from the Latin limen, "threshold". Finally, incorporation: the community takes you back with your new status. The middle is the strange part. Picture standing in a doorway: out of one room, not yet in the next.

cards.headline: Coming of age
cards.body: Bar and bat mitzvah mean "son" and "daughter of the commandment". Jewish boys usually mark it at 13 and girls at 12 or 13, often with a first public reading from the Torah. In the 20th century the bat mitzvah for girls spread widely, across Conservative, Reform and some Orthodox congregations.

cards.headline: The last rite
cards.body: Hindu funeral rites, antyeshti, vary by caste and sect, but generally involve cremation and placing the ashes in a sacred river. For 10 days the immediate family observe special restrictions and perform rites that many Hindus believe help the soul of the dead on to its next life. A rite of passage, it turns out, carries the living too.

cards.headline: Rites of Passage: the takeaways
learned: Rites of passage move people from one status to another
Van Gennep's three stages: separation, transition, incorporation
A bat mitzvah and a Hindu funeral both follow the pattern

questions.prompt: Rites of passage were named and described in 1909 by _____.

options.label: Emile Durkheim
options.rationale: He wrote on religion and community in 1912.

options.label: Edward Tylor
options.rationale: He defined religion by belief in spiritual beings.

options.label: Ninian Smart
options.rationale: He described seven dimensions of religion.

questions.explanation: The French anthropologist Arnold van Gennep introduced the term in 1909.

questions.prompt: Put van Gennep's three stages of a rite of passage in order.
questions.explanation: First comes separation from the old status, then transition, the liminal stage, and finally incorporation into the community with the new status.

questions.prompt: After a Hindu cremation, the family observes 10 days of special restrictions. Which stage does that period match?

options.label: Separation, before the rite begins
options.rationale: The death and cremation are the separation.

options.label: Incorporation, the return to daily life
options.rationale: Incorporation comes once the restrictions end.

options.label: None: funerals aren't rites of passage
options.rationale: Van Gennep counted death rites among them.

questions.explanation: The 10 days sit between the death and the family's return to daily life: the liminal, transition stage.
